steps.step: A filter's bits are fixed entirely by the items added to it. Bit i is 1 exactly when at least one added item has i among its k positions. The order of adds does not matter.
steps.part: How it works: add and query
steps.idea: Adding an item only sets its k positions (hash mod m) to 1 and keeps nothing else. Bits start at 0 and are never cleared (see also 'Why it is never wrong the other way').

steps.step: Because the two filters have the same m and the same k hash functions, any item gets the same positions in both. So bit i in filter A is 1 when some item of A maps to i, and bit i in filter B is 1 when some item of B maps to i.
steps.part: How it works: add and query; Not covered here (Growing: changing m changes every position)
steps.idea: Positions come from the hash output mod m. With the same hashes and the same m, the positions line up. With a different m they would not.

steps.step: A bitwise OR of the two arrays gives bit i = 1 exactly when some item of A or some item of B maps to i. That is the same as when some item of A ∪ B maps to i. This is exactly the array you would get by adding every item of A ∪ B to an empty filter.
steps.idea: Building from A ∪ B sets the union of the bits that A's items set and the bits that B's items set. OR computes that union of bits.

steps.step: So the OR is exact: it matches the A ∪ B filter bit for bit. It has no false negatives, and its false-positive rate is that of a filter holding |A ∪ B| items. If the union goes over capacity, that rate rises.
steps.part: Step 3; Why it is never wrong the other way; How often it is wrong; Overfilling
steps.idea: The OR filter is a normal filter for A ∪ B, so the usual guarantee and the rate p ≈ f^k apply, with n equal to the number of items in the union.

steps.step: A bitwise AND gives bit i = 1 when some item of A maps to i and some item of B maps to i. Every item in A ∩ B has all k of its bits set in both filters, so the AND keeps them. As a filter for A ∩ B, it never says 'definitely not seen' for an item that is in both sets.
steps.part: Steps 1–2; Why it is never wrong the other way
steps.idea: An item in both sets set its own bits in each filter, and bits never go back to 0.

steps.step: The AND is not exact. A bit can be 1 in A because of one item and 1 in B because of a different item. For example, take A = {cat} with bits 1, 6, 11 and B = {owl} with bits 3, 6, 11. The AND has bits 6 and 11 on, but A ∩ B is empty, and its true filter is all 0s. So the AND can have more 1s than the A ∩ B filter, and it gives extra false positives.
steps.part: How it can be wrong: false positives (owl shares bits 6, 11 with cat); How it works (cat's positions)
steps.idea: Bits do not record which item set them. Two different items can share positions, so a shared 1 does not mean a shared item.

result: OR the two bit arrays. You get exactly the filter you would have built from A ∪ B: every bit is the same, it has no false negatives, and it has the normal false-positive rate for |A ∪ B| items. A bitwise AND gives a filter that still has no false negatives for A ∩ B, but it is not exact. It can have 1s where different items of A and B happened to share a position, so it is at least as full as the real A ∩ B filter and gives more false positives. The explanation does not give a formula for how much more.
